summary:
SPHEREx Explorer is a public-facing web tool that makes NASA’s infrared sky observations easier to explore and compare over time. Users search by sky coordinates or object name, filter observations by detector group, and play chronological image sequences. A dedicated comparison view aligns observations onto a shared sky-coordinate grid, helping users inspect possible positional changes relative to surrounding stars.

An interactive sky map displays observation footprints over reference imagery, while Gaia DR3 and AllWISE catalog overlays provide additional context. Users can export comparisons as videos, and an AI assistant explains observation metadata and scientific limitations.

By connecting real archive data with an accessible visual workflow, the project lowers technical barriers to participation in astronomical exploration. It supports the investigation of possible changes without claiming automatic discovery confirmation.
details:
SPHEREx Explorer addresses the challenge of making infrared sky observations accessible for public investigation of changes over time.

Users enter Right Ascension and declination, resolve an astronomical object name, or select a position on an interactive sky map. The application queries NASA/IPAC IRSA for SPHEREx observation metadata and retrieves the associated scientific FITS files. The backend validates the image extension and creates browser-viewable PNG previews.

The application offers two complementary viewing modes. Full-frame playback presents observations chronologically with detector-group filtering and adjustable speed. Aligned comparison resamples two observations onto a common WCS-based tangent-plane grid, using the same centre, scale and orientation. Users can inspect the images side by side or blink between them, view their observation dates and time separation, and export date-labelled WebM videos.

Aladin Lite provides sky navigation over clearly labelled AllWISE infrared and DSS2 optical reference imagery. SPHEREx footprints show observation coverage. Gaia DR3 and AllWISE catalog markers provide cross-mission context in the comparison panels. Gaia positions are approximately propagated to the observation date when proper-motion information is available.

Sky Assistant uses Groq to explain astronomy, application features and the selected comparison metadata. Responses are streamed and formatted with Markdown. The assistant receives metadata rather than image pixels and is instructed not to claim visual detections or confirmed discoveries.

The frontend uses Next.js, React, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS. The Python backend uses FastAPI, Uvicorn, Astropy, NumPy, SciPy and Pillow. Requests and HTTPX support external service communication.

Performance measures include a priority queue with up to three concurrent preview requests, shared frontend preview caching, lazy-loaded gallery images, next-frame preloading, backend caching and cancellation of obsolete browser requests. Aladin’s HiPS viewer loads image detail progressively according to zoom level.

The project is a visual exploration tool, not a calibrated photometry or automatic discovery pipeline. Display normalization, wavelength differences, quality flags and residual astrometric errors must be considered when interpreting apparent changes. External archive availability can also affect live queries.

Development priorities include documented validation on the five challenge targets, tighter wavelength matching, quantitative motion measurements, calibrated photometry and more resilient hosting.
